built_by: Hand-maintained registry, in the same style as _data/channel_facts.json and _data/taxonomy.json: it holds prose and URLs, never a count. Every count on the entity page is counted from the collection data files by Liquid at build time, so this file cannot make the page publish a figure the data does not support.
purpose: The registry behind /asadullah-ali-al-andalusi/ and /asadullahali-com-what-happened/. It exists because those two pages have to state facts that are not in any collection file - which name forms are attested, where, and by whom - and a page that states such facts without recording where each one came from would be exactly the kind of claim this archive refuses to make.

external_check.how: HTTP HEAD, no query string, no credit-spending API, no search engine. Eleven URLs.
external_check.why: A link-out is a citation. The archive's standing rule is that a URL is printed only when something established it; an unverified URL is not printed, and a URL that is printed carries the status it was given on the date it was checked.
external_check.statuses_are_point_in_time: Every status below is the response on the date above and nothing more. None of them is a claim about what the host will do tomorrow.

disambiguation.other_person_also_called: a separate, active Muslim speaker, London-based, who runs his own site and channel under that name
disambiguation.external_check_note: Both of the other person's own properties answered HTTP 200 on 2026-09-28, so the two names are live at the same time and the confusion is current rather than historical.
disambiguation.why_the_two_appear_together_in_this_corp: Because the author himself writes about the other man in the third person. In the recovered work `whataboutery` (2015), whose text is preserved in this repository and published verbatim, the author describes `MDI representative Abdullah Al-Andalusi` as someone else in the room: `...her frequent interruptions, appeals to emotion, question begging, and her shouting over MDI representative Abdullah Al-Andalusi as he was comprehensively detailing the cruel oppression of state actors...`. The same post carries the tag `Abdullah al Andalusi`. That is the archive's own primary evidence that the two are two people, and it is stronger than any external source, because it is the subject distinguishing them in his own published words.
disambiguation.the_mislabelling_runs_both_ways: Four preserved recording titles in _data/videos.json name `Abdullah al Andalusi` or `Abdullah Al-Andalusi` for recordings this archive attributes to Asadullah Ali, and four more rows record in their own `source` field that the recording was placed with him by a sweep of the muslimdebate.org byline, where the byline reads `The Big Atheism-Theism Debate: Dr. Arif Ahmed vs Abdullah al-Andalusi`. In every one of those eight rows the attribution rests on the byline, not on the name in the title, and the row says so.
disambiguation.the_gate: The archive's byline gate is the thing that keeps the two apart, and it is a rule rather than a judgement: a row counts as his on the strength of the byline the publishing site records, and never on the strength of a name in a title. Concretely - all 17 rows in _data/mdi_articles.json carry `author: Asadullah Ali Al-Andalusi`, recovered from the MDI author archive under author id 16585639 with the byline verified as `Asadullah Ali`; and the eight rows named above record their basis in the row's own `source` field. The rule is written down and executable in scripts/apply_taxonomy.py, which stamps `category` and `counted` on every countable row from the data and can be re-run with `--check` to prove nothing drifted. It is the same principle the archive applies everywhere else: the assignment is computed from evidence and re-checkable, not asserted.
disambiguation.why_it_is_printed_here: Because the collision is the reason a search for one name returns the other, and because a page that silently resolved it would be making a claim the archive can support only for rows it has actually measured. A reader looking for the other man should reach a page that tells them plainly that this is the wrong one, rather than a page that quietly credits him with someone else's work.

queries.a: It was the author's own website and the original home of The Andalusian Project's writing. The site is defunct. The domain no longer belongs to him: it now resolves and serves an unrelated, commercially operated gambling site, and it should not be visited. This archive does not control the domain and does not claim to represent it.
queries.short: It was his site. It is defunct, the domain has since been taken over by an unrelated gambling operation, and it should not be visited.

queries.a: The Andalusian Project's site was asadullahali.com, with a WordPress mirror at asadullahali.wordpress.com. Both are effectively gone as a place to read the work: the first domain is hijacked, and the mirror is still up with its post bodies removed.
queries.short: The site was asadullahali.com plus a WordPress mirror. One is hijacked; the other is an empty shell.

queries.a: Yes, and the archive states why per item rather than in summary. Every recovered work carries the Wayback capture it was recovered from, so a citation resolves to what was actually written rather than to a site that no longer serves it.
queries.short: Yes. Every recovered work carries the dated capture it came from, so the citation still resolves.

queries.a: Two properties existed: asadullahali.com and the WordPress mirror asadullahali.wordpress.com. The first is hijacked and is printed here as plain text only. The second is still up but its post bodies have been removed. This archive holds the recovered work with per-item provenance.
queries.short: asadullahali.com is hijacked; the WordPress mirror is up but emptied. The recovered work is here, with provenance.

queries.a: That is the correct description and it is not a fault on the reader's side. The domain resolves and answers, which is exactly why a link to it is dangerous: it returns a live page that has nothing to do with him. Follow the Wayback capture recorded on each page here instead.
queries.short: Correct, and not your fault. The domain answers - with someone else's site. Use the recorded captures.

queries.a: The videos are gone. The channel id continued to exist and was captured repeatedly, so the archive holds a dated record of what it showed, and 68 catalogued recordings with their ids, durations and surviving copies. Most of the recordings are preserved as files in the Internet Archive's andalusian-project collection, and 68 of them have machine transcripts published here.
queries.short: The videos are gone. 68 recordings are catalogued, most preserved on the Internet Archive, with 68 transcripts here.

queries.q: what happened to the andalusian project
queries.a: Three separate things, and the archive keeps them apart because they are not the same event. The written work was scattered across Wayback captures, an Internet Archive directory, a live third-party site and an emptied WordPress shell, and has been gathered here with per-item provenance. The video channel lost its videos around October 2022 and its history is recorded capture by capture. The original domain was taken over. Nothing here says the author stopped writing; it says where the published work is and where it is not.
queries.short: The writing was scattered and is gathered here; the channel lost its videos in 2022; the domain was taken over.
